recent_posts.title: ACCU on Sea : The 2026 Schedule is Here!
recent_posts.summary: The full schedule for ACCU on Sea 2026 has been announced. The main conference runs June 17–20 across five tracks, covering C++23/26, reflection, contracts, async patterns, memory layout, performance, and software design. Pre-conference workshops on June 15–16 include sessions on C++ Best Practices (Jason Turner), C++ Templates (Walter E. Brown), C++23 in Practice (Nicolai Josuttis), Unsafe Rust, Secure Coding in C/C++, and a Speaker Training Workshop. Evening events include lightning talks, a welcome reception, Movie Night with pizza, and a gala conference dinner. ACCU on Sea hoodies are available as a new add-on this year. Keynotes from Andrei Alexandrescu, Yvonne Rogers, and Walter Brown are confirmed, with a fourth keynote to be announced.

BeCPP Symposium 2026 - Herb Sutter - C++ Growing in a world of competition, safety, and AI
recent_posts.summary: Herb Sutter's keynote at BeCPP Symposium 2026 covers three structural changes affecting C++: power constraints driving demand for performance-per-watt languages, evolving software security landscape, and AI's impact on programming. C++ grew 74% in the last 3 years, outpacing the average 50% growth across all languages. The talk argues that memory safety is only 3 of the top 10 software vulnerabilities, that C++ is safer than C when distinguished properly, and that C++26 ships meaningful safety improvements (initialization safety, hardened standard library, contracts) with minimal overhead. On AI, Sutter argues it reduces drudgery and helps with long-tail bugs but won't replace human programmers, drawing parallels to Visual Basic's democratizing effect. Hyperscaler CapEx on power (~$700B across 5 companies in 2025) directly benefits performance-focused languages like C, C++, and Rust.

recent_posts.title: AI-generated C++ code that looks optimized but performs poorly
recent_posts.summary: A deep dive into AI-generated C++ code from the 'markus' project (a Markdown-to-HTML parser created with Claude Opus), revealing how vibe-coded C++ can look optimized but perform poorly. Key issues uncovered include: a fake SIMD-friendly loop that's actually slower than a simple single-loop implementation, inefficient case-insensitive string comparisons that create multiple temporary strings, memory waste from using std::variant with wildly different-sized types (128 bytes per node just to store a space), redundant NodeType enumerations, and several PVS-Studio-flagged bugs like unnecessary copies instead of moves and double hash-map lookups. Benchmark results show the 'optimized' nested-loop version is the worst performer of all tested variants. The author argues that expert code review remains essential precisely because AI-generated code can superficially mimic optimization patterns while hiding serious inefficiencies underneath.

recent_posts.title: Devirtualization and Static Polymorphism
recent_posts.summary: Virtual dispatch in C++ enables runtime polymorphism but introduces overhead through vtable indirection, larger object sizes, and missed inlining opportunities. Compilers can sometimes devirtualize calls automatically using flags like -fwhole-program and -flto, or via the final keyword. When devirtualization isn't possible, static polymorphism via CRTP (Curiously Recurring Template Pattern) resolves calls at compile time with zero runtime cost. C++23's 'deducing this' feature offers a cleaner alternative to CRTP by templating only the member function rather than the entire class, achieving the same optimized output without the boilerplate.

recent_posts.title: C++: Some Assembly Required - Matt Godbolt - CppCon 2025
recent_posts.summary: Matt Godbolt's CppCon 2025 closing keynote weaves personal history — from ZX Spectrum BASIC and ARM assembly on the Archimedes, through games industry C++ and finance trading — into a broad tour of why assembly language still matters for C++ developers. He live-demos Compiler Explorer showing how GCC and Clang compile a hex-string validator at O1/O2/O3, explaining x86, ARM, and RISC-V register conventions and ABIs. He also previews a new Claude-powered 'explain assembly' feature in Compiler Explorer. The second half surveys the C++ ecosystem: the STL's origin story via Stepanov, Boost as a standardization proving ground, the new Beman project, and the fragmented landscape of compilers, editors, build systems, and package managers.

recent_posts.title: Beyond Sequential Consistency: Unlocking Hidden Performance Gains - Christopher Fretz - CppCon 2025
recent_posts.summary: A CppCon 2025 talk by Christopher Fretz exploring C++ memory ordering models and their practical performance implications using a lock-free ring buffer as a benchmark. Starting with sequential consistency (the default), the talk demonstrates a ~17x throughput improvement by switching to acquire-release semantics, eliminating lock-prefixed atomic instructions on x86. Further gains come from cache-line alignment to prevent false sharing, yielding nearly 20x total improvement. The talk also covers why undefined-behavior workarounds (volatile + compiler fences) work on x86 but fail on ARM due to platform-specific memory ordering guarantees, validating the importance of std::atomic. Bonus material covers cached index snapshots to reduce cross-core cache invalidation, pushing throughput even higher.

recent_posts.title: vittorio romeo's website
recent_posts.summary: An early benchmark analysis of C++26 reflection's compile-time overhead using GCC 16. Key findings: the -freflection flag itself adds zero overhead, but including the <meta> header costs ~155ms per translation unit. Standard Library headers like <print> and <ranges> are the real bottleneck, not the reflection logic itself. Precompiled headers (PCH) are effectively mandatory for scaling, cutting AoS-to-SoA compile times from 818ms down to 113ms. C++ modules currently underperform PCH for smaller headers but are comparable for large ones like <print>. The author also notes a correction from an earlier version where a debug-build GCC Docker image inflated all numbers by ~40-50%.

recent_posts.title: Using C++26 reflection to auto-generate Python bindings for trading algorithms
recent_posts.summary: C++26 static reflection can eliminate the manual boilerplate required to bridge C++ and Python in algorithmic trading systems. Using Bloomberg's Clang P2996 fork, a compile-time loop inspects class members and auto-generates Python bindings via PyBind11, letting you run computationally heavy models like the Merton Jump Diffusion pricer at native C++ speeds while keeping strategy logic in Python. The approach is demonstrated with a live market-making bot on BitMEX, and a full proof-of-concept repo is available on GitHub.

recent_posts.title: Introduction to SDL3 graphics programming for C++ game developers
recent_posts.summary: A CppCon 2025 talk by Mike Shah introducing SDL3 (Simple DirectMedia Layer) for C++ game developers. Covers SDL3's cross-platform value proposition, basic window creation and event handling, 2D rendering with surfaces and textures, hardware-accelerated rendering via the SDL renderer, and the new SDL GPU API that provides a higher-level abstraction over Vulkan, Metal, and Direct3D 12. Includes live demos showing window creation, sprite animation, and GPU-rendered quads. Also touches on shader basics (vertex, fragment, compute), SPIR-V compilation, and the broader question of whether C++ should have a standard graphics library.
